2. The opposite party was a tenant under the plaintiff at a monthly rent of Tk. 25/- payable according to the Bengali calendar month in pursuance of a Bharanama dated 18th Jaistha 1369 B.S. Bharanama, Ext. 1, shows that the suit premises was leased out to the opposite party for one year from 1st Jaistha 1369 B.S. to 30th Baisakh 1370 B.S. Defendant opposite party agreed to pay rent each month on or before the 3rd day of the following month. He paid rent up to Chaitra 1381 B.S. Thereafter he defaulted in the payment of rent. Plaintiff requires the suit premises bonafide for constructing a staircase. Opposite party having refused to vacate the suit premises the petitioner served a notice Ws. 106 of the Trans of Property Act but the notice which was sent by registered post came back with the endorsement of the peon "refused" on it. Thereafter the petitioner filed the suit for ejectment of the opposite party. 

 4. The learned S.C.C. Judge found that the opposite party has filed some challans showing deposit of rent, Ext. B series, but he has not filed the challah by which he deposited the rent for the month of Baisakh 1382 B.S. Be that as it may, the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party contended at the time of trial that the defendant deposited rent for the month of Baisakh on the 4th of Jaistha and not on the 3rd of Jaistha as stipulated in the Bharanama Ext. 1. The learned S.C.C. Judge noticed that the Bharanama, Ext 1, was only for one year. The alleged default for Baisakh 1382 B. S. therefore took place long after expiry of the period of lease. The learned S.C.C. Judge took the view that the, tenant opposite party held over as a tenant after the expiry of the term of lease. He continues with the tenancy not under the same terms and conditions as in the Bharanama, Ext. 1 but under the general laws of the country. Under the general law, he opines, the tenant opposite party can deposit rent within the 15th of the month next following that for which it was due and therefore the deposit on the 4th Jaistha was within time. The learned S.C.C. Judge there-fore held that the tenant opposite party was not a defaulter. Regarding the bonafide requirement of the landlord petitioner the learned S.C.C. Judge came to the finding that the plaintiff has got a was served genuine need of the suit premises and it is not a mere fancy. With regard to the notice u/s. 106 of the Transfer of Property Act the learned S.C.C. Judge noted that the tenant opposite party has contended that no registered letter was tendered to him, that he did not refuse to accept any letter and that no notice was served legally upon him, Taking the view that the endorsement "refused" on the registered notice, Ext. 4, must be formally proved by the postman who wrote it and endorsed it or by any other competent person who knows the handwriting of the postman, the learned S.C.C. Judge found that the said endorsement has not been formally proved in this case and no evidentiary value can be attached to it. He therefore held that Transfer of Property legally served upon with these findings dismissed the suit, the Act the notice u/s. 106 of the had not been duly and tenant opposite party learned S. C. C. Judge 

 5. Mr. Abdur Rahim, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned S. C. C. Judge acted illegally and with material irregularity in assuming that the opposite party deposited the rent for the month of Baisakh 1382 B. S. on the 4th of Jaistha, merely upon the submission of the learned Advocate for the tenant-opposite party and not on the basis of evidence on record. He submits that the defendant-opposite party has adduced evidence by producing challahs that he deposited rent from Jaistha 1382 B. S. onwards in the Rent Deposit Case No. 176/ 75, but he has given no evidence whatsoever that he deposited rent for the month of Baisakh 1382 B. S. Mr. Rahim submits that the decision of the learned S. C. C. Judge that the tenancy of the opposite party will be guided by the general laws of the country after expiry of the period of one year's lease is uncalled for. The opposite party has not proved that he paid rent or deposited rent for the month of Baisakh 1382 B. S. 

 7. In his examination-in-chief the opposite party deposing as D. W. 1 did not specifically say that he deposited rent in R. D. Case No. 176/75 for the month of Baisakh 1382 B. S. He only said that he offered the rent for the month of Baisakh but the landlord refused to accept the same. No money order receipt has been produced to show that the landlord refused to accept rent for the month of Baisakh. No challan has been produced to show that the rent for Baisakh was deposited in R. D. Case No. 176/75. The landlord-petitioner as P. W. 1 has of course stated in cross-examination that the opposite party deposited rent of Baisakh and onwards in the said R.D. Case but he also stated that the deposit was not proper and legal. When it is the positive case of the landlord that the tenant did not pay rent from a particular month it is for the tenant to adduce evidence to show that he paid rent in accordance with the contract or in terms ' of the provisions of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. The opposite party has not furnished any evidence in this regard. The learned S.C.C. Judge has taken note of the submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party that the opposite party deposited rent for the month of Baisakh on the 4th of Jaistha. This was only a submission not based on any evidence on record. The further findings of the learned S. C. C. Judge that the tenancy of the opposite party will be governed by the general laws of the country after expiry of the period of lease contained in Bliaranama Ext. 1, was beside the point. Clearly the opposite party having failed to adduce evidence that he paid rent for the month of Baisakh was a defaulter in the payment of rent for that month. 

 11. In two other decisions involving service of concise statement under the Bengal Tenancy Act and the service of notice under the Bengal Agricultural Tenancy Act it was held that where a notice addressed to a person and sent by registered post is returned to the sender with an endorsement "refused' by the postman, the notice would be presumed to have been duly served upon the addressee without the examination of the postman or other evidence regarding tender and refusal. Those are the cases of Sita Nath Mondal v. Soleman Adolk, (2) and Nirmal Bala Debi v. Provat Kumar Basu, (3) respectively.
